sec.title: Background
sec.p: Adavosertib is a highly selective, small molecule Wee1 inhibitor that sensitizes tumor cells to cytotoxic agents.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: We report results from the lead-in cohorts of two phase II studies: carboplatin/pemetrexed plus adavosertib versus carboplatin/pemetrexed in first-line metastatic non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (NCT02087241); and docetaxel plus adavosertib versus docetaxel in recurrent NSCLC (NCT02087176).

sec.title: Patients and Methods
sec.p: Both lead-in cohorts assessed early safety and efficacy (objective response rate [ORR]). First-line metastatic treatment was carboplatin (area under the curve to 6 h [AUC6]) plus pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1, every 21 days; recurrent treatment was docetaxel 75 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1 plus prophylactic granulocyte-colony stimulating factor 6 mg subcutaneously on day 4 every 21 days. All patients received adavosertib 225 mg twice daily orally on days 1–3 (five doses). After a planned safety analysis of the first-line trial, dose and schedule were modified to reduce toxicity.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: First-line: 14 patients were enrolled in four treatment cohorts. Median time on trial was 17.3 weeks, with an ORR of 29%. The most common adverse events were diarrhea (50%), nausea (50%), vomiting (50%), anemia (43%), neutropenia (43%), decreased appetite (43%), and dehydration (43%). Recurrent: 32 patients were enrolled. The ORR was 9%. The most common adverse events were diarrhea (66%), anemia (50%), nausea (47%), fatigue (47%), vomiting (44%), and thrombocytopenia (41%).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Both studies terminated early; the recurrent study after an interim analysis showed increased toxicity and limited efficacy, and the first-line study after a change in first-line standard of care.

tr.td: Adavosertib plus docetaxel showed poorer tolerability than expected with docetaxel alone in patients with refractory non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
A trial of first-line adavosertib plus pemetrexed in patients with metastatic non-squamous NSCLC was discontinued because of a change in standard of care to immunotherapy.
Adavosertib has been investigated in various solid tumors, both as monotherapy and in combination with chemotherapy, targeted agents, and immunotherapies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Lung cancer is the leading cause of malignancy-related mortality worldwide [1]. The prognosis for patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains poor, even with the incorporation of immunotherapy into the treatment paradigm for all patients with NSCLC [2–4]. Prior to immunotherapy, first-line treatment options for advanced NSCLC were limited and associated with poor outcomes; pemetrexed plus platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin or carboplatin) doublet chemotherapy was among the standard-of-care options [5]. When immunotherapy with or without chemotherapy became standard of care for all patients with newly diagnosed NSCLC, docetaxel re-emerged as one of several standard systemic options for use after progression from first-line therapy. Docetaxel was used as a benchmark comparator versus pemetrexed in a non-inferiority trial in which progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) in the docetaxel arm were 2.9 months and approximately 8 months, respectively, with an overall response rate of 9% [6]. Given that an efficacy plateau had been reached with traditional chemotherapy combinations in NSCLC, there was increasing interest in combining chemotherapies like docetaxel with the newest generation of targeted therapies, with the goal of improving efficacy with manageable toxicity [7].

Adavosertib is a highly selective, adenosine-triphosphate competitive, small-molecule inhibitor of the Wee1 kinase that sensitizes tumor cells to cytotoxic agents. Wee1 plays an important role in cell cycle regulation and DNA damage repair; therefore, inhibition of Wee1 may increase the effectiveness of DNA-damaging treatments, such as chemotherapy, by forcing tumor cells with damaged DNA to enter mitosis, ultimately leading to tumor cell death [8]. Adavosertib has been investigated for the treatment of advanced solid tumors as monotherapy and in combination with chemotherapy [9–13]. Here, we report efficacy and safety results from the lead-in phases of two subsequently terminated trials of chemotherapy plus adavosertib in NSCLC: a phase II trial of carboplatin and pemetrexed plus adavosertib in first-line metastatic non-squamous NSCLC, and a phase II trial of docetaxel plus adavosertib in patients with refractory NSCLC.

sec.title: First-line Adavosertib plus Pemetrexed in Patients with Metastatic Non-squamous NSCLC
Study Design
sec.p: This randomized, phase II trial compared adavosertib plus pemetrexed and carboplatin followed by maintenance adavosertib plus pemetrexed with pemetrexed and carboplatin followed by maintenance pemetrexed in patients with metastatic non-squamous NSCLC that was untreated in the metastatic setting (NCT02087241). The safety cohort described in this article was included to enable a preliminary assessment of safety before randomization. The primary endpoint of the planned randomized component of this trial was PFS, and secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), duration of response, OS, and the safety profile of the adavosertib combination treatment.

sec.title: Eligibility
sec.p: Eligible patients were treatment naïve (with the exception of adjuvant therapy, provided the interval from adjuvant therapy until disease progression was > 12 months) with recurrent or stage IV advanced non-squamous NSCLC and the ability to swallow oral medication. Patients with TP53 mutations and wild-type tumors were eligible; patients with known activating mutations in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) or rearrangements in anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) were not eligible. Patients with prior radiation to the whole pelvis or to > 25% of the total bone marrow area were also excluded. Radiation therapy had to be completed > 2 weeks prior to enrollment. Patients had measurable disease according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST, version 1.1) [14], an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) score of 0 or 1, and adequate organ and bone marrow function.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: The original treatment regimen was adavosertib (225 mg orally [PO], twice daily [BID]) on days 1–3 at approximate 12-h intervals for a total of five doses (once daily on day 3) with pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 and carboplatin area under the curve (AUC) to 6 h (AUC6) intravenously (IV) on day 1 of a 21-day cycle (cohort 1). Patients continued all study treatments until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. To minimize myelosuppression with the triplet combination, adavosertib dosing was amended to five doses of adavosertib 225 mg PO BID on days 3–5 (cohort 2), and then to five doses of adavosertib 175 mg PO BID on days 3–5 (cohort 3). Finally, the treatment regimen was amended to five doses of adavosertib 125 mg PO BID on days 1–3, pemetrexed 400 mg/m2 IV, and carboplatin AUC to 5 h (AUC5) IV on day 1 (cohort A). Prophylactic antiemetics (dexamethasone 8 mg [PO BID] and ondansetron 8 mg [PO BID]) were administered on each day of adavosertib dosing.

sec.title: Adavosertib plus Docetaxel in Patients with Refractory NSCLC
Study Design
sec.p: This phase II, randomized, open-label, multicenter trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of adavosertib and docetaxel in previously treated patients with advanced NSCLC. The lead-in cohort described in this article was included to assess early safety and efficacy.

sec.title: Eligibility
sec.p: Eligible patients had histologically or cytologically confirmed advanced NSCLC (excluding large-cell neuroendocrine and mixed NSCLC/small-cell histologies) and had progressed on or discontinued one prior platinum-based doublet treatment for advanced NSCLC. Patients with TP53 mutations and wild-type tumors were eligible. Patients with a known EGFR mutation or ALK translocation had to have received a previous platinum-based chemotherapy doublet as well as either an EGFR or ALK inhibitor, respectively. All patients had the ability to swallow oral medication and had adequate bone marrow, kidney, and liver function. Patients with known central nervous system metastases were eligible if the metastases were stable and had no evidence of progression or hemorrhage after treatment for > 2 weeks prior to enrollment. Patients with Class ≥ 2 cardiac disease were excluded.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: Patients received adavosertib (225 mg PO BID) on days 1–3 at approximate 12-h intervals for a total of five doses in combination with docetaxel (day 1, 75 mg/m2 IV) with 6 mg concomitant subcutaneous prophylactic pegfilgrastim on day 4 for the prevention of febrile neutropenia. Premedication with antiemetic therapy was allowed and was based on the institution’s standard practice of the administrating physician. Medications were also allowed to be administered for maintenance of existing conditions prior to study enrollment or for a new condition that developed while on the study. Trial treatment was administered in a 21-day (3-week) cycle until disease progression or intolerable toxicity.

sec.title: Interim Analyses (Both Trials)
sec.p: Two interim analyses were planned during the trials. The first analysis, conducted by a safety review team, occurred after the first six evaluable patients in the safety lead-in completed one cycle of treatment. The frequency and severity of safety events were compared with published data, in the same setting, for pemetrexed and carboplatin administered as doublet therapy and for docetaxel administered as a single agent. A second interim analysis in both trials was planned to assess tumor response and cumulative safety when at least 20 patients had their first tumor response assessment after two cycles of treatment. The assessment involved an interim conditional probability analysis with simultaneous sample size re-estimation, [15] based on PFS time during the randomized part of the study and conducted by an independent statistician. Futility would be assessed when approximately 27 (33%) of the 82 planned events had occurred. In conjunction with the futility analysis, an unblinded safety review would be conducted that investigated adverse (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs), medical histories, concurrent illnesses, and changes in clinical laboratory parameters and vital signs.

sec.title: Pretreatment Evaluation (Both Trials)
sec.p: Before the initiation of trial treatment, all patients underwent a complete medical history, physical examination, complete blood counts, chemistry profile, and assessments of ECOG PS and concomitant medications. Tumor staging evaluation included computerized tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen/pelvis, positron emission tomography (PET) scan or PET/CT scan, and CT or magnetic resonance imaging of the brain.

sec.title: Safety and Efficacy Assessments (Both Trials)
sec.p: All patients who received at least one dose of protocol treatment were assessed for toxicity. All AEs and SAEs, regardless of relationship to trial treatment, were collected from the first dose to 30 days after discontinuing treatment. Toxicities were graded according to the National Cancer Institute’s Common Terminology for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 4.03 [16].

Patients were assessed for tumor response every two cycles (6 weeks) for the first year and every four cycles (12 weeks) thereafter, until documented objective disease progression as defined by RECIST version 1.1 [14]. The ORR includes all patients with either a complete (CR) or partial response (PR) per RECIST version 1.1.

TP53 mutations, identified retrospectively using next-generation sequencing of either archival or fresh tumor tissue, were defined as missense mutations that result in < 20% of wild-type TP53 transactivation activity; mutations that result in 20–50% of transactivation and are observed ≥ 20 times in the somatic mutation list; a dominant negative mutation, stop codon, or frameshift mutation prior to codon 306; or consensus splice site mutations prior to exon 8. Transactivation activity data were downloaded through an International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) TP53 database [17]. Activity was measured using a yeast-based functional assay that analyzed the transaction activity of all possible TP53 missense mutations on eight different TP53 response elements in TP53 target genes: BAX, CDKN1A (WAF1), GADD45A, MDM2, P53AIP1, PMAIP1 (NOXA), RRM2B (P53R2), and SFN [18].

sec.title: Statistical Analysis (Both Trials)
sec.p: The trials required ≥ 20 evaluable patients to fully power the interim analysis of the ORR. Twenty patients were considered sufficient to provide a reasonable level of precision for estimating the true rates. Based on the upper bounds of one-sided 90% confidence intervals for these rates, and the likelihood that the true ORR is at least 0.40 and/or the true DCR is ≥ 0.75, as well as the safety profile of the treatment combination at the time of response evaluation, the randomized part of the study could be initiated. For both studies, the primary endpoint was PFS. For the patients with refractory NSCLC, 82 events would provide at least 85% power to test the primary hypothesis using a one-sided, log rank test at the 0.10 significance level. For treatment-naïve patients, with 80 events, the study would have at least 85% power to test the primary hypothesis using a one-sided, log rank test at the 0.10 significance level. The evaluable efficacy analysis population included all patients receiving at least one full or partial cycle of the treatment regimen and for whom measurable disease at baseline was established. The safety analysis population consisted of all patients who received at least one dose of investigational drug. The objective ORR was defined as complete or partial tumor response according to RECIST version 1.1 criteria [14]. Disease control was defined as a patient achieving a CR, PR, or stable disease (SD) according to RECIST version 1.1 criteria [14]. The investigator-reported tumor response per time point was listed, including the percent change from baseline and percent change from nadir in sum of longest diameters of target lesions. A waterfall plot of best percent change in sum of longest diameters from baseline (including cohort/arm and dose) was generated.

sec.title: Ethics and Consent (Both Trials)
sec.p: The trials were conducted according to the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and were approved by the institutional review boards of each participating site. All patients provided written informed consent prior to trial enrollment.

sec.title: First-line Adavosertib plus Pemetrexed in Patients with Metastatic NSCLC
sec.p: Fourteen patients were enrolled and treated in four cohorts with varying doses and schedules of adavosertib: three in cohort 1, three in cohort 2, one in cohort 3, and seven patients in the final cohort (cohort A). Most patients were Caucasian (92.9%) and female (57.1%). The median age was 63.0 (range 46.0–81.0) years, with 42.9% of patients being 65 years or older. All patients were current or former smokers. The demographics and key baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Tissue was collected for assessment of TP53 mutations at enrollment from seven patients. Of these, four patients (57.1%) had TP53 mutations and three (42.9%) had no TP53 mutations detected.

sec.p: The trial was discontinued early due to adoption of chemoimmunotherapy as the first-line standard for all patients with metastatic NSCLC.

sec.title: Adavosertib plus Docetaxel in Patients with Refractory NSCLC
sec.p: Thirty-two patients were enrolled. Most patients were Caucasian (87.5%) and male (59.4%). Twenty-nine patients (90.6%) were smokers, one patient (3.1%) was a non-smoker, and two patients (6.3%) did not report their previous tobacco use. The median age was 62.0 (range 36.0–76.0) years. TP53 status was available for 27 of 32 patients (84.4%), 17 of 32 patients (53.1%) had eligible variation TP53 mutations (eligible variation criteria are defined in Table 1), three of 32 patients (9.4%) had non-eligible variation TP53 mutations, and seven of 32 patients (21.9%) had no TP53 variation. The demographics and key baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1.

sec.title: First-line Adavosertib plus Pemetrexed in Patients with Metastatic NSCLC
sec.p: The overall median time on trial was 17.3 (range 2.7–68.4) weeks, with a median of four (range 1–18) cycles (Fig. 1). Median (range) times on adavosertib, pemetrexed, and carboplatin were 10.6 (0.3–64.6), 10.4 (0–28.3), and 9.1 (0–12.7) weeks, respectively.

sec.p: Ten patients (71.4%) discontinued all trial treatment and 11 patients (78.6%) discontinued pemetrexed and carboplatin. Of the ten patients who discontinued all trial treatments, four patients were withdrawn due to either patient or physician decision (28.6%), two patients (14.3%) were withdrawn due to AEs, two patients (14.3%) progressed on the trial, and two patients (14.3%) died. Four patients (28.6%) continued to receive treatment with adavosertib at the time of data cut-off, including three patients who also continued to receive pemetrexed and carboplatin.

sec.title: Adavosertib plus Docetaxel in Patients with Refractory NSCLC
sec.p: The overall median time on trial was 5.4 (range 0.4–29.4) weeks, with a median of two (range 1–10) cycles (Fig. 1). Median (range) times on adavosertib and docetaxel were 5.4 (0.3–29.1) and 4.4 (0.1–29.1) weeks, respectively.

At the time of data cut-off, 29 patients (90.6%) had withdrawn from trial treatment and three patients (9.4%) continued to receive treatment with adavosertib and docetaxel. The main reasons for treatment discontinuation were disease progression (nine patients, 28.1%), patient decision (six patients, 18.8%), AEs (five patients, 15.6%), death (four patients, 12.5%), physician decision (four patients, 12.5%), and other (one patient, 3.1%).

sec.title: First-line Adavosertib plus Pemetrexed in Patients with Metastatic NSCLC
sec.p: The best overall tumor response (and ORR) during the trial was four patients (28.6%) with PR and six patients (42.9%) with SD (Table 2 and Fig. 2). One patient (7.1%) had progressive disease, and three patients (21.4%) were not evaluated (one patient died and two patients withdrew from the trial prior to disease assessment). Of the four patients with TP53 mutations, the best overall tumor response was one patient (25.0%) with a PR and three patients (75.0%) with SD.

sec.title: Adavosertib plus Docetaxel in Patients with Refractory NSCLC
sec.p: All 32 patients (100%) were included in the efficacy population (17 patients TP53 eligible, three TP53 non-eligible, seven no TP53 variation, and five no result available). Three patients had a PR; thus, the ORR was 9.4%. All three patients that achieved a PR by RECIST version 1.1 had TP53 mutations (Table 2). One patient had additional mutations in EGFR, one had mutated Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene (KRAS), and the third responding patient had no other significant gene mutations. Twenty-one patients (65.6%) had SD, and ten (47.6%) of these patients had TP53 mutations. Consequently, a total of 24 patients (75.0%) achieved disease control (DCR; CR + PR + SD), and 13 (54.2%) of those patients had TP53 mutations. Of the eight patients who were not in the disease control population, four (50.0%) had TP53 mutations (Table 2). A waterfall plot of maximum change from baseline in target lesions is presented in Fig. 2.

sec.title: First-line Adavosertib plus Pemetrexed in Patients with Metastatic NSCLC
sec.p: All patients experienced at least one AE during this trial, and 13 patients (92.9%) experienced a treatment-related AE (TRAE). The most common adavosertib-related AEs were nausea (50.0%), diarrhea (42.9%), vomiting (42.9%), anemia (42.9%), neutropenia (42.9%), thrombocytopenia (35.7%), and dehydration (35.7%). The most common treatment-emergent AEs are presented in Table 3. Five patients (35.7%) experienced dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) (cohort 1: grade 3 diarrhea, grade 2 vomiting; cohort 2: grade 3 vomiting, grade 4 neutropenia; cohort 3: grade 2 acute kidney injury; all n = 1). Ten patients (71.4%) (including one patient with an SAE who fell outside the scope of “treatment-emergent,” and one patient with an SAE that occurred after database lock) experienced at least one SAE (grade 3 atrial fibrillation; grade 5 intracranial bleed; grade 3 influenza; grade 5 failure to thrive after treatment discontinuation; grade 3 neutropenic fever and grade 3 stroke; grade 3 diarrhea, vomiting, and mucositis/mucosal inflammation; grade 4 mucositis, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia, and decreased platelet count plus grade 3 dehydration, upper gastrointestinal tract bleed, and hypokalemia; grade 5 gastrointestinal hemorrhage and dehydration; grade 4 neutropenia and grade 3 abdominal pain; AE of grade 3 cholecystitis, which was recorded by safety monitoring, but occurred after data cut-off; all n = 1).

sec.p: There were five deaths on trial: two due to disease progression, one TRAE (treatment-related dehydration and gastrointestinal hemorrhage), and two treatment-emergent SAEs (intracranial hemorrhage and failure to thrive).

sec.title: Adavosertib plus Docetaxel in Patients with Refractory NSCLC
sec.p: All patients experienced at least one AE, and 31 patients (96.9%) experienced an AE considered related to adavosertib by the investigators. Seventeen patients had SAEs (53.1%). Twelve patients (37.5%) had an SAE related to adavosertib: two of those patients discontinued trial drug treatment and two died. One patient experienced grade 2 abdominal pain during cycle 1 that was considered a DLT.

The most common adavosertib-related SAEs were grade 4 thrombocytopenia, grade 3 abdominal pain, grade 3 nausea, and grade 3 asthenia, each of which were reported in two patients (6.3%). Overall, four patients (12.5%) discontinued the trial due to AEs. Two patients discontinued treatment due to SAEs considered related to adavosertib (grade 3 nausea and grade 3 gastrointestinal bleeding). Two additional patients (6.3%) discontinued treatment due to an AE related to adavosertib.

The most common treatment-emergent AEs were diarrhea (65.6%), anemia (50.0%), thrombocytopenia (40.6%), nausea (46.9%), fatigue (46.9%), and vomiting (43.8%) (Table 4). Twenty-four patients (75.0%) experienced a grade ≥ 3 treatment-emergent AE.

sec.p: Sixteen patients (50.0%) in the safety population died: nine patients (28.1%) due to progressive disease; five patients (15.6%) had an SAE with the outcome of death (two patients with respiratory failure, one patient each with febrile neutropenia, failure to thrive, and hemorrhage); and two patients (6.3%) died as a result of unknown causes.

sec.title: Second Interim Analysis (Adavosertib plus Docetaxel in Patients with Refractory NSCLC)
sec.p: Results from the second planned interim analysis suggested that toxicities associated with adavosertib given in combination with docetaxel were greater in frequency and severity than with docetaxel alone, especially gastrointestinal and hematologic toxicities. Furthermore, analysis revealed that it was unlikely that the target response rate would be reached in the trial. It was therefore decided that the randomized phase of the trial would not commence, and the trial was discontinued early.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Combining adavosertib with standard chemotherapy (carboplatin and pemetrexed) in first-line metastatic NSCLC resulted in overlapping hematologic AEs as well as enhanced gastrointestinal toxicities. As a result, all three drugs were dose attenuated and given with an adjusted schedule. Furthermore, early closure of the carboplatin and pemetrexed with adavosertib in the first-line metastatic NSCLC trial did not allow comparison with pemetrexed and carboplatin without adavosertib. The small patient population also prohibited determining whether the presence of a TP53 mutation could identify patients who would benefit from the addition of adavosertib to chemotherapy. Of 14 patients enrolled and treated, ten (71.4%) discontinued all trial treatment. With an increase in time on the treatment regimen, efficacy may have increased above that seen in this trial. However, the combination of adavosertib and carboplatin has shown encouraging efficacy rates in select patients with TP53-mutated ovarian cancer that was refractory or resistant to first-line therapy within the first 3 months of initial treatment, and in combination with paclitaxel plus carboplatin in patients with TP53-mutated platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer [19, 20].

Hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicities were observed after combining adavosertib with docetaxel in recurrent NSCLC. In particular, neutropenia was still observed despite the mandatory administration of pegfilgrastim. The three patients with PRs and ten of the 21 patients with SD had TP53 mutations; however, TP53 mutations were not exclusive to responders and numbers were too small to confirm if this population derives enhanced efficacy. The high rate of toxicity (75.0% experienced grade ≥ 3 AEs) and discontinuations (12.5% discontinued due to AEs) made it difficult to fully evaluate the efficacy of the drug combination.

While the treatment landscape for NSCLC is rapidly changing, the appetite for novel targeted agents and drug combinations has never been greater. Therapies targeting mutations in EGFR, ALK, ROS proto-oncogene 1 receptor tyrosine kinase (ROS1), v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B1 (BRAF), and others have shown great promise for treating patients in the target populations [21]. If the toxicity observed in these trials can be ameliorated, adavosertib may be another targeted agent with efficacy for select NSCLC patients; biomarkers of sensitivity would need to be explored.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In summary, no conclusions were possible following discontinuation of first-line adavosertib plus pemetrexed in patients with metastatic non-squamous NSCLC because of the change in standard of care to immunotherapy. Adavosertib plus docetaxel given in the lead-in period in patients with refractory NSCLC showed poorer tolerability than expected with docetaxel alone and was considered unlikely to reach the targeted response rate.
